newsitem.title: FRANCE: France spells out NATO demands, plays down US row.
newsitem.headline: France spells out NATO demands, plays down US row.

text.p: France on Tuesday played down its differences with the United States over NATO reforms, saying its demands that the alliance's European regional commands be put under European officers had been misconstrued.

Foreign Minister Herve de Charette wrote in a newspaper article that France was not asking for the command of the alliance's vital southern flank, nor did it want the U.S. Mediterranean Sixth Fleet to come under foreign command.

The article was published in the Paris-based daily International Herald Tribune as NATO's 16 foreign ministers met in Brussels to review internal reforms necessary for the alliance's expansion plans in eastern Europe.
"France wants the two regional European commands assigned to European officers on a rotating basis," de Charette wrote.

He said that since Washington insisted that NATO's two supreme commanders remain Americans, it seemed fair that the two regional European commands, including the southern command AFSOUTH, be assigned to European officers on a rotating basis.

"The new political and strategic realities in Europe amply justify that regional commands be manned by European officers, but we are aware of the special strategic role played by the Sixth Fleet, not only for NATO missions but also for the defence of American national interests," de Charette went on.

NATO's reform plans have been held up by the row over who is to command AFSOUTH. The issue of U.S. forces being commanded by a foreigner is a sensitive one in the United States, and ever since the alliance was set up in 1949, a U.S. officer has held the Naples-based southern command, which carries with it control of the U.S. Sixth Fleet.
De Charette said France had always made clear that arrangements should be devised for the Sixth Fleet to remain under U.S. control, even if the AFSOUTH commander was European.
Such arrangements existed for the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps which was under the direct command of the alliance's American supreme commander, he said.

"What it boils down to is that France, supported by some of her key European partners, deems it necessary, since the United States keeps the two strategic command positions, that the next level of command in Europe be attributed to European officers on a rotating basis while deferring to key U.S. interests in the Mediterranean," he said.
Paris has hinted that the issue could delay its plan to rejoin NATO's military structure, which it left 30 years ago, and in turn delay the alliance's expansion plans.
